newsitem.title: FINLAND: Finns head for polls with hint of Euro-doubt.
newsitem.headline: Finns head for polls with hint of Euro-doubt.

text.p: Finns deliver a verdict on the European Union on Sunday when they vote in their first European parliamentary elections, with a tint of Euro-scepticism creeping into an otherwise bland picture.

Party support remains little changed with backing for the pro-Europe government coalition partners unshaken, but personal support for the most visible opponent of the EU, and especially of a single European currency, has suddenly picked up.
Esko Seppanen, a vocal left-wing Euro-sceptic, has become the most popular individual candidate, backed by almost 11 percent of the electorate, opinion polls say.
Finland joined the European Union with Austria and Sweden in January 1995 after a referendum in which 57 percent of the electorate voted for membership.

It is now directly electing members to the Strasbourg-based parliament for the first time. It will have 16 deputies there, chosen from 207 candidates in balloting twinned with local government elections.
The vote comes one week after Finland linked its currency to Europe's stability mechanism, major step towards a single currency.
Only Seppanen, a rogue member of the Left Wing Alliance, a member of the governing coalition, has made this a campaign issue.
Opinion polls say less than one-tenth of Finns feel very negative about EU membership but about 60 percent oppose a single currency.

"I think Seppanen is collecting all the votes against (the EU) -- in a way, the nationalist vote," said fellow candidate Ralf Sund. The party of former communists and leftist socialists has not stood on a nationalist platform.
With the turnout expected to be low, perhaps 50 to 60 percent against 70 percent in a general election, no-shows by apathetic voters could paint a more anti-European picture than has emerged so far.
The press has dubbed the election the "celebrity poll" since an Oscar-winning filmmaker and an Olympic gold-medal skier are still polling well alongside political heavyweights.
But Social Democrat Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen's five-party coalition apparently faces no serious upset in either election.
"It looks like Lipponen can calmly wait for the results... There's no spirit of protest in the air," said the daily Helsingin Sanomat in an editorial.
A survey for television news on Friday gave 26.5 percent of the vote to his party, with the main opposition Centre Party, only ever half-heartedly anti-Europe, a clear second with 22.5 percent.
